utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Muireann Dennehy, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, and legal intern Ze-emanuel Hailu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have a minor procedural issue that we'd like to address. I do apologise, I believe my microphone is working but it doesn't seem to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: We indicated last night that the Prosecution would like to request an additional 30 minutes of time in order to present this witness's evidence in-chief. The Defence has raised no objection in relation to the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Unless there's something further from the Prosecution, I do have a comment to make on this. Mr. President, there's no objection to the additional time, as such. However, we did receive a proofing note last evening. I don't recall the exact time but it was after 6.00. And most of the material in the proofing note is -- falls within the scope of what has been indicated in the witness statement and the witness summary. But there are some items that go beyond the witness summary and the witness statement which was the only indication that we had of the content of the witness's expected testimony until last night at 6.30. One of the items of new information is innocuous but -- or relatively innocuous, but we're still going to make an objection on principle when the issue comes up, and some of the other items are not so innocuous. I understand from my learned friend that they will not be leading that new information. But nonetheless, I just thought I should say for the record that although there is no objection to the additional time, there may be an objection to the manner in which that additional time is being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, do you need that additional time for the new information or is there no connection between the two?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the additional time relates primarily to the number of documents that we're seeking to tender through this witness. It does not relate to the additional information that was given to the Defence last night in the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If I may, we indicated this morning early that the additional information to which the Defence objects will only be referred to by way of background. We won't lead testimony in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning -- good morning, Mr. Witness. Good morning, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Pero Coric. I was born on 28th of April, 1962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Can I now ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Ms. Dennehy, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may ask for the assistance of the court usher, please. This is a numbered hard copy of the witness's statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Coric. Can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, do you recall giving a statement to the representatives of the Tribunal in December 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Turning to tab 5 of the Court's bundle, can I please ask the English version of 65 ter 2221.1 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, do you recognise the document in front of you to be the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: From what I see on the cover page, I suppose that this is the same document that I have recently seen. The only thing is I can't see my signature. This is a copy, I suppose. And I suppose that this is the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. If you look at the screen in front of you, on the left-hand screen you will see the English version of your statement. Can you please tell me whether you now recognise any of the signatures on the bottom right-hand corner of that English version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, I can see my signature in the right-hand side bottom corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And before coming here today, did you have a opportunity to review your statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And during that review, you identified a number of minor errors in your statement which I would now like you to correct. Looking at the front page of your statement, can you please tell the Court your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Currently, I'm a politician.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now, looking at paragraph 3 of your statement at line 3, where it notes that the council consisted of 24 representatives. What correction would you like to make to that number?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: My correction would be this: In 1995, when I provided this statement, I was speaking from memory, and I said that there were 24 representatives. However, when I returned to Vukovar, I perused some documents, and I was able to establish that there were actually 25 representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now looking at line 6 of that paragraph where it states: "However, the council met only once ..." what correction would you like to make to the term "council"?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: At that time I didn't say, or perhaps I did by mistake, it was not the council but the joint municipality of Vukovar, which had three councils, one was the social and political council that I was a member of. There was a -- the council of local communes that Goran Hadzic was a member of. And the last council was the council of associated labour. So when I said "the council" here, I didn't actually mean the council but the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar as whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. And, finally, looking at paragraph 4 of your statement where you referred to the man known as Bratus, can you please tell me what amendment you would like to make to that line?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: In Sarengrad, which is a place where I come from, people are known by their nicknames. One of them was a person known as Bratus. Later on, I inquired about his name and I learned that his name was Milivoj Radojcin.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Coric, that you have made these corrections, if I were to ask you the same questions that you were asked in 1995 when you met the representative of the Tribunal, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and the accuracy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 2221.1. That is, the numbered reference of the witness's statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you just told the Court that you were a professional politician. What political party did you establish?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: In 1989, I was the founder of the HDZ or the Croatian Democratic Union. And now, for four and a half years I have been active in another party that I founded four years ago. We are a party in the parliament. We have a representative in Brussels who is a member of the European Parliament, the name of my party is the HSP Dr. Ante Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 3 of your statement you say that you were chosen as a representative of Sarengrad and Mohovo to the Social Political Council in the democratic elections in 1990. When did you first encounter Goran Hadzic in this role?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. There is no mention of Goran Hadzic in the witness's statement and there's no mention of Goran Hadzic in the summary provided for this witness. And the only mention we have is in the proofing note that arrived last night at 6.32 p.m. And once this question is asked, then other questions are going to be asked that will lead to more substantive issues of which we have no notice. So that's our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I indicated in an e-mail to the Defence this morning, this information will be only be used by way of background. The primary focus of the witness's evidence will be that that is related in the witness summary relating to the events in Sarengrad. The Defence is correct insofar as this information was provided in the proofing note circulated late last night, but that is the first indication that the Prosecution received of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, when you say "by way of background," having regard to the substance of the objection which the Defence has made, I confess I'm somewhat confused as to what you propose to do with this new information of which the Defence has not had notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to lead evidence in relation to this to outline the witness's political background and his political experience in Vukovar around the time of the democratic elections in 1990. As I indicated earlier, there were only be a few handful of questions in relation to the accused and his activities. The primary focus of this witness's evidence will be the events in Sarengrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But doesn't this go to the heart of the Defence objection to this evidence being there at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. As I noted earlier the -- we did provide this information as soon as the Prosecution was made aware of it and that was then circulated in the proofing note late last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, having heard Ms. Dennehy's explanation, do you maintain your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I certainly do, Mr. President. The -- the excuse for the -- or the explanation given for the late notice is unconvincing. The Prosecution has had 18 years to take a subsequent statement from this witness. An investigator could have interviewed the witness six months or a year ago. That would have provided us with an opportunity to discuss the matters that are addressed in the proofing note with our client. We don't have a translation of the proofing note. That means that there's been no consultation with the client based upon a careful review of what's actually in there. The Prosecution doesn't need this information to come from this witness because Your Honours already have plenty of background information, if that's the purpose for the information coming in. And if you look at the statement, Mr. President, there's absolutely nothing incompatible in having the witness describe what he knows as expressed in the statement without any reference to Mr. Hadzic. That's what's in the statement already. So the Prosecution doesn't even need this information for the witness's testimony to be a coherent whole. So, on those grounds, Mr. President, yes, we do maintain the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Please proceed, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, at paragraph 3 of your statement, you said and you clarified earlier that the Vukovar Assembly met only once after the Borovo Selo incident in -- on the 2nd of May, 1991. Can you tell me why the Vukovar Assembly met only once?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Barricades had been erected. The Bloody Easter happened on the 31st of March, 1991. The person present here, Goran Hadzic, was arrested in Plitvice as well at the other persons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The name escaped the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then we started an initiative to hold a joint Assembly, speak to the media, condemn violence, and to establish what was going on and whether people were really carrying arms and so on and so forth. Obviously the Serbian side that had a majority in -- at the Assembly in Vukovar and Goran Hadzic was one of the loudest among them, the Assembly broke up and never -- was never reconvened after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you've just told the Court that there was an initiative to condemn the violence. Can you tell me more about that initiative in relation to the Vukovar Assembly.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I've just said that, unfortunately, Mr. Goran Hadzic and like-minded persons to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. We're now getting into a situation where the witness has heard the objection and obviously is determined to provide the information he wishes, notwithstanding the ruling. So given that, I would respectfully an instruction from the Chamber to the witness not to embark on a discussion of those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you heard the first objection made by the Defence. You heard the Trial Chamber's ruling and the second objection by the Defence. Could you please try to respect what we decided until now and stay within the limits of your statement and answer the questions the Defence is putting to you -- sorry, the OTP is putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm not a lawyer, so I do not understand when I overstep the boundaries. In paragraph 3, I provided a very succinct statement and I believe that the Trial Chamber should be provided with additional information from me as an active protagonist of the events. I have to say that those events were the starting point of everything that subsequently happened in Eastern Slavonia. That's why I said in my statement, i.e., in the annex to that statement, that the SDS party that Goran Hadzic headed did not participate in the first democratic petition -- elections.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to slow down. It is impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Witness, there's another slight problem. The interpreters don't follow you. You're speaking too fast. Could you please slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As I've already said, the party that was headed by Goran Hadzic, the SDS, did not participate in the first democratic elections in East Slavonia or in Vukovar. They appeared at the elections as the Communist party. They turned coat the following day and they became the SDS. That's how they gained an apparent majority in that body, and that body later on made subsequent decisions that resulted in war and aggression against that part of Croatia. This is what I stated in paragraph 3. At that joint Assembly we tried to achieve peace, to condemn every form of violence and to appear as such before the people who had elected us. We wanted to tell them that we would do our utmost to stop any further aggression and erecting of barricades. We wanted all of us to get an insight into the arms depot that was under the control of the TO Vukovar. Unfortunately, it was then under the control of the SDS, Goran Hadzic, and the others who were in the Assembly. We were never given an opportunity to see what was going on with the military equipment. Once we reached those depots, which were finally emptied, we are convinced that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now the prejudice, Mr. President, the prejudice has just been caused because that was precisely the allegation, which is contained nowhere in the witness's statement, that was of concern to the Defence. The allegation is untrue. And yet we're in a position where we're learning about it the night before the witness's testimony, at 6.30 p.m. And Your Honours have heard it. Your Honours are professional Judges, and I have complete confidence in your ability to reject that from your consideration. But it does put the Defence in a dilemma. I'm not sure what would the best -- what the best manner of proceeding is, but at the very least, I think we now should move on to the next part of the statement, which is paragraph 4, and not dwell on the subjects that are currently being testified to by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, we would instruct you to move on and to control the witness with regard to our ruling. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Coric, we will now move on to the defence activities that you were involved with in Sarengrad. At paragraph 4 of your statement, you described that a civilian defence force was established in Sarengrad and that you were the one appointed in charge of that force. Can you please tell the Court what duties did you have as head of the civilian defence force in Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It was called civil protection in those days. There have been no roadblocks in Sarengrad ever. There was no need for them. Neither the Serbian minority nor the Croatian majority erected any. We were all oriented toward co-existence, but because we were uninformed, we didn't know what was going to happen. We expected to be attacked by infantry, by sabotage detachments who would come at night to kill people and burn down houses. That's why the civil protection was organised. There was a round-the-clock duty -- there were round-the-clock duty shifts, and two to three people should be awake at any time and monitor what was going on in the village so as to be able to alarm all of us in case of need so that we may protect the people and their property. That civil protection was an organisation based on volunteering. We were around 100 volunteers who didn't have any military training or military equipment. We mostly had hunting rifles. Everything we had was kept at the local commune facilities. Nobody carried it home or gave -- gave the weapons to any patrols.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I have also mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. I'd like to ask you a number of questions about what you've just told the Court. You said that you had mostly hunting rifles. Did you have any -- sorry. You had mostly hunting rifles. Were these weapons sufficient to defend Sarengrad against a potential JNA attack?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Of course, not. As a military layman, I had no idea what kind of weapons we would be faced with and what kind of power -- what kind of forces would be used against bare-handed people. It wasn't anywhere present in our minds that -- that the so-called JNA would side with the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that on the 5th of September, 1991, the JNA surrounded the village of Sarengrad. How did the people in the village react to the JNA surrounding it?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Paragraph -- paragraph 7. You say: "On the 5th of September, 1991, the JNA surrounded our village." My question is: How did the people in the village react to this surrounding by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It was somewhere in the month of July. It became obvious that the JNA was an aggressor army. On the 16th of July, a Croatian police officer was killed on duty on the bridge. He was in a police car near Ilok. His name was Goran Stipak. The JNA had already attacked some nearby places and we understood that they were our enemies. On the 5th of September, the last road was cut. I think that somebody from Sarengrad was in Vukovar on that day for the last time. Until that time, communication was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Can you please tell us how the people in Sarengrad reacted to the JNA? And just focus on that question in particular, please.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I said that for us the JNA was beyond doubt an aggressor army who cut us off from any medical assistance or other logistics such as food supply or supply of medication. What the people in the village, including me, heard and saw having been able from -- to escape from them were horrible things. They used heavy weapons to target some places and they were coming from the direction of Celije where some villages had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. Now, in your statement you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, unless I missed it, I didn't hear an answer to your question about how the people reacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can put that question again if it would help.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, as you have heard Your Honour say, you haven't provided specific information as to how the people in Sarengrad reacted to the JNA. You described that you were cut off from medical assistance and other logistics, such as food supply. But how did the people react?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: There were no JNA members at Sarengrad or near the village. But they were a few kilometres away. They were surrounding us, attacking us from time to time so that our attitude toward the JNA was very clear: It was an enemy army and there was no doubt about it. I can say that the prevailing emotion toward the JNA was fear. Those days, they were already targeting our church and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. Now you describe on the 4th and 5th of October, 1991, how shells -- how the JNA attacked Sarengrad. How many shells fell on Sarengrad during the first day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my statement, the attack started soon after 12.00 on the 4th of October, 1991. Before that, there had been attacks against Ilaca, Tovarnik and other nearby places, and thousands of people were fleeing towards Ilok. They were all passing through Sarengrad. There, there had an attack by tanks because it's a plain, and we didn't expect an infantry and tank attack but the opposite happened. On that day, mortar shelling began from the direction of Backa Palanka, so they were shooting over the Danube, from Bent, from smaller calibre mortars. The tanks were positioned at Pajzos, between Sarengrad and Bapska, and they were targeting visible targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Due to the very limited time that we have in court this morning, I would like you to focus on my specific question. And that question was: How many shells fell on the first day?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: According to our estimate, on the first day, as many as 1500 shells of various calibres fell on our village on that first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how many days did the shelling last for?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: The most intensive shelling was on the 4th of October, until evening hours. After that, it continued for five or six days where there was sporadic shelling. So if anybody was moving along the Danube, whenever they saw a car moving, mortars fire began or fire from anti-aircraft guns and all possible weapons until the end, at least 500 shells of various calibres had hit the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. I'd like to now show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 365, that's at tab 15 of the Court bundle, be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You'll see this document appear in front of you, Mr. Coric. Mr. Coric, this is a JNA military document. At page 1 it states: "On 4 October 1991, division units shall be engaged in carrying out the following tasks ..." And now looking at page 2, under paragraph 4, the different types of units involved in the proposed attacks are described. Those are a Howitzer battalion, an anti-aircraft battalion, and an artillery rocket battalion. My question is: In your experience of the attack on Sarengrad, were these the types of weapons used to attack the village?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. These very Howitzers were shooting at us and the anti-aircraft guns were at Bent near the Danube. They were used to shoot at the houses near the Danube and all other visible targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. And now scrolling back up to page 1 of that document, the date of that document is the 4th of October, 1991. Can you please tell me, was this the first day of the attack on Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender 65 ter 365 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I wasn't aware of the fact that it was an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Coric, I would now like to show you a video-clip and you'll see that appear on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 5033.2 be shown and, for the record, this is a video-clip with time stamp 11:35 to 13:36. And I would please ask my Case Manager to pause the video at 13:36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just inquire whether I have received -- whether the Defence has received the video by way of DVD or CD?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my Case Manager informs me that this video was disclosed but a copy is on its way to the Defence for their records. This was also on the exhibit list, circulated over two weeks ago and has been on each draft exhibit list since.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not perhaps exactly sure what is a practice and what is a rule. Normally in practice we do receive the videos by way of CD. I don't dispute that it's been disclosed. So I'm in Your Honours' hands as to whether you would wish to proceed, even though we haven't received the version on a CD directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, can you tell me what this means to you in fact? So you -- it is disclosed. It is on the exhibit list. But you don't have a CD. Are you able to see it in preparation or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As I sit here in court, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I cannot as I sit here in court in advance. Of course, it will be shown on the screens and we'll all be able to look at it together. I -- in all honesty, Your Honours, I can't tell you whether or not -- I'm not sure whether we could have pulled it out of our disclosure and looked at it separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's amazing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It may be amazing, Mr. President, but often these things are just handed to you. You don't the procedures or the mechanics, and so that's why I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: "Ilok is rare, a small pleasant town in Eastern Croatia untouched by bullet, bomb or shell. But the war has emptied its streets. Over half the predominantly Croat population fleeing after the federal army and the Serbs took control, leaving behind shattered homes and streets, where only the occasional chimney betrays a sign of life. "Traffic is monopolised by the military ferrying supplies to the front lines, first at Vukovar, now around Osijek. Amongst those who stayed, there is much talk about the Blue Helmets, UN soldiers who Mr. Vance wants to deploy to end the war - a hope they share. But there is also as clear a disagreement amongst the civilians and soldiers as amongst the politicians as to precisely where they should be sent. "I think it would help. If the Blue Helmets came here, many of the Croats who fled would be able to come back. "I think the Blue Helmets shouldn't come here at all. If they did, it would only lead to a return of the Croat extremists. "The Blue Helmets could stop this war but only if they deploy in what we see as the true border of Serbia, and that's beyond the current front lines. "A standard view amongst the soldiers and Serb militiamen that the war has not yet been fought to its true conclusion and that even a UN deployment would not bring it to an end. "The farmers of the neighbouring village of Sarengrad are still harvesting their corn. They are late - a consequence of too little manpower, a consequence of war. The village has survived. It was less fortunate than Ilok, and Croats like Tomislav Sabo who've remained are bitter, speaking of property and livestock being confiscated. "They've got to go to the Croatian borders as they were when this war began."

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, on the video in front you, did you recognise the towns depicted in that video?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to recognise the tanks. But I recognised the places and the people in the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what were those places in the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: If I may say, the one that you can see now, if we're looking at the same image, the church behind this man is the Orthodox church at Sarengrad, which was targeted from the other side of the Danube, and it was destroyed. So they destroyed their own church. And the other places that we saw were the school and the fire-fighters' building. And the man driving the tractor whose name is Tomislav Sabo, I know him. He stayed behind in Sarengrad by chance but he was tortured badly, beaten up. He had to go to work camps. Today he is almost deaf, blind, and unable to work. That's a consequence of the beatings he suffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that this clip is already in evidence. I've just been provided with that information now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do apologise. I've just been informed that in relation to the Defence's previous objection, I have been told that this clip was provided to them in respect of a previous witness so they did have a copy in their possession quite recently. I was very much mistaken when I said this evidence -- this clip is in evidence already. I need to tender this clip, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now ask that 65 ter 414 be shown to the witness. That's at tab 2 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: This is a collection of documents, Mr. Coric, relating to October 1991. Looking at page 1 of this document, and page 1 is in English version of this document, this is a letter written by Marin Vidic to the ECMM, the European Community Monitoring Mission. Do you know Marin Vidic?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him, both privately from the war, and we're friends today.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: In -- on page 1 of this document, it says: "The eastern part -- the JNA increased its activities in the eastern part and with no direct reason destroyed Bapska, Sarengrad and Lovas." In your experience, is that what happened to those towns?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to see this document. I think that it's accurate, fully accurate. Without any reason these places were attacked, and some 15.000 civilians were already crammed in the city of -- in the town of Ilok. And I believe that the final number was a bit higher still.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. Now looking at page 3 of this document, again, this is a letter to the ECMM dated October 15, 1991. I don't believe you have a B/C/S version in front of you. However, I will read parts of that document to you and it will be translated. On page 3 it says: "In the agreement it is listed that on the basis of a so-called local population referendum, those citizens from the area who so desire to emigrate will be allowed to do so." And at paragraph 1, that document mentions Ilok, Bapska, and Sarengrad. Can you tell me, did a referendum take place in Ilok; and can you describe what that referendum related to?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: The referendum took place on the 13th of October, 1991. I had the opportunity to see this document. The word "negotiate" is not an appropriate term. Because you can't really speak of negotiations. That was a package of ultimatums issued by the JNA and the paramilitaries who ordered us the following: You will either leave Ilok, Bapska or Sarengrad or be killed. Of course, the outcome of the referendum was clear. The people who were in Ilok all could vote. It didn't matter whether they were residents of Ilok or not. 95 per cent voted in favour of leaving Ilok and they wanted members of the Croatian police to accompany them at least with side weapons. In that ultimatum, safety was promised to all who decided to leave, but, of course, they didn't have the right to take valuable property with them. Whoever did was left without it. Many people were beaten up on the spot and a large number ended up in camps. The ultimatum was issued by the JNA, and the citizens of Ilok voted at the referendum in favour of leaving to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would tender this document at this time. That's 65 ter 414.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We object to that, Mr. President. The document appears to be -- I'm -- I would say of 25 pages long. There are a range of different documents that appear to be attached together under the same 65 ter number. Some of them are dot-matrix printouts of possibly news reports. It's not clear where they came from or how they are related to the first two documents that have just been shown to the witness. So we would suggest that the appropriate -- and if we just look at the front page of this 65 ter document, you can see that there is a -- a paper clip photocopied on the front page and it says faintly at the top "annex A" and the second document may say "annex B" at the very top, which suggests that these are two annexes that were attached to a cover page that is not part of the document. So what I would say is that these two documents that have been shown to the witness should be split up into two separate 65 ter numbers and then can be admitted on that basis separately without the other documents attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Seems reasonable, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the purpose of my questions to the witness were to provide sufficient foundation for this entire document. It is, in fact, a series of documents received from the ECMM and that was indicated on the draft exhibit list circulated two weeks ago and again last Thursday and again last night. So the nature of the document is clear insofar as it is a compilation of documents but it was received, and it relates to the ECMM mission in October 1991 in Sarengrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Received by whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Received by the OTP. If it would assist the Court, I can go to a number of documents subsequent to the one that I addressed with the witness. However, he has provided information that would assist the Court and find it -- in providing a foundation for those subsequent documents in his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if that is the case, if that's the reason for tendering these documents together as a bundle, all the more reason why they shouldn't be admitted. Your Honours don't have the cover page. We don't have an ECMM witness in front of us, even though they have been called and presumably there will be more to come. And this witness is certainly not in any position to explain how these documents are interconnected in relation to whatever the cover page may have been. And I would suggest in respect of some of the other attachments that again this witness is not in the position to explain how they are interrelated, and that now seems to be what the Prosecution is trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, either you split the document and tender the two documents separately, or you try to establish a nexus between the other documents and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think at this time the best solution would be to split the documents as the Defence has suggested and tender each of them separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Admitted and marked as such.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not quite sure of the mechanics and I've displayed my utter ignorance of mechanics, so if I could just inquire, I don't know what's just been admitted specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So just -- just to make things clear, Ms. Dennehy, we're talking about the two documents you showed the witness; right? Now we would need two -- two separate 65 ter numbers for them, and then we'll give, Madam Registrar, I suppose, two separate exhibit numbers. Or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will give them two separate numbers then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The second number therefore is P2278. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you describe the referendum that took place in Ilok and the subsequent convoy that left Ilok. Turning to tab 1, that's exhibit 371.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can I ask that 65 ter 371 please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You will see an agreement. And in the first paragraph of that exhibit, it was states the -- it was agreement between the authorised representatives of the people of Ilok, Sarengrad, and Bapska. Do you recognise the agreement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I don't have it on the screen yet. Now I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I recognise it. When it was drafted, I knew about it. All the proposals that we tabled were turned down. And I know all the people who participated. I believe that there is a mistake here. The name is not Mate Bristic but Mate Brletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And in your experience, was this agreement drafted on 14th of October, 1991, as indicated in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time we would like to tender exhibit 65 ter 371 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now ask that 65 ter 2241 please be shown. That's at tab 4 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you'll soon see a document on the screen in front of you. And these are excerpts from the minutes of the Ilok Urban Community Assembly Session held on the 6th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The 65 ter is 2241. I apologise, 2214. And that's at tab 4 of the Court's bundle. It's also Exhibit P321.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, on page 2 of this document, you see the name M. Bosnjak. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. Marinko Bosnjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when he says, "They intend to enter Ilok and they'll do it. If a decision on handing over the weapons is made, they will come and carry out a massacre." Who is the "they" that Marinko is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, who were the residents of Ilok expected to hand over weapons to?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: There was a team of people who went to negotiate with the so-called JNA. They came to pick them up in Ilok and sometimes they took them to Backa Palanka and other times they took them to Sid. My deputy, the late Ivan Groznica Ivsa, participated instead of me, and they took them on purpose through various units. Before the negotiations they had an opportunity to see thousands upon thousands of the JNA soldiers, of the so-called JNA, and thousands upon thousands of volunteers. They had an opportunity to see hundreds of tanks, cannons and Howitzers. This obviously instilled fear in them, and people who came back spoke about crimes that happened in Lovas and further afield that compounded the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Coric. You mentioned that you knew Marinko Bosnjak. Who was this man?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object now on basis of lack of notice. I don't see any indication in the witness's statement or the summary of the subject matter of this testimony. Maybe I can be directed by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this refers to the evacuation of Ilok and the convoy that left Ilok and it's referred to at paragraph 11 of the witness's statement in relation to the refugees that left Sarengrad for Ilok. And I also intend to refer to a further subject that is mentioned in this document, namely, the visit of the ECMM to Sarengrad, and that is referred to at paragraph 13 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I may be confused but when I look at the minutes, this seems to be a discussion of the evacuation of Ilok, not the evacuation of Sarengrad. So -- and -- and this witness was not a participant. He was not a member of the convoy evacuated from Ilok. In fact, it's not clear from the statement what his knowledge of that might be. Or -- or of these minutes, so ... at least based on the information I have, it does appear to be outside the scope of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: First question, Ms. Dennehy, is this about Ilok or about Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the part of the document to which I've referred, refers to Ilok. But in the witness's evidence, he speaks to the evacuation of Sarengrad which, in turn, leads into the evacuation of Ilok. If it would assist the Court, I can show a map that shows the proximity of those two villages. It is witness's general evidence there was an evacuation of the area of Eastern Slavonia rather than specific villages within it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You wanted to say something, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. The issue is not physical proximity. The issue is two different events. And the issue that the minutes are speaking to is the lead-up to and the circumstances of the evacuation of Ilok town. And I presume that that's what these minutes are about. And curiously, there's no mention in the witness's statement of the circumstances or the details of the evacuation of Ilok town, because he left by a different means. And he certainly doesn't mention any meetings of the town of Ilok council to discuss how, when, why, that should occur. So, for those reasons, it falls outside of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. You may proceed, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, if you could answer the question again. The Marinko Bosnjak who you speak of, can you please tell me who this person is?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Can I say just one sentence? Ilok is divided into four places. Sarengrad is one part of Ilok. It was then in 1991 and still is. In regional terms those four parts are connected. Marinko Bosnjak was an elderly person, a private shop owner from Ilok. He was one of the commanders in the civilian protection. I believe that his opinion was based on the experiences that he had heard from the tens of thousands of people who had fled into Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. Now moving down on that page, you see that, further down this next paragraph, the European Economic Community's Monitoring Mission is mentioned and a Mr. P Cobankovic says that: "The ECMM does not guarantee us security but that they could help with the eventual evacuation of women and children. They went to Sarengrad ..." In your statement, you say that you went to Ilok to get the ECMM monitors. Is the same visit of which Mr. Cobankovic speaks of the one that you arranged?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I explain? I actively participated in the drafting of all the documents and passing of all of the decisions in Ilok. I did that through my deputies. I was in Sarengrad all the time because people were vulnerable there, some were wounded. There was a lot of cattle killed, a lot of houses burning. I couldn't be in Ilok all the time. On that day, on the 10th, was the first time after the attack that I arrived in Ilok because my deputies had informed me that they saw an ECMM vehicle and several people in white uniforms. They asked -- we asked them whether -- we asked them whether they would arrive in Sarengrad and places that were directly attacked and where there were casualties, dead, and wounded, and destruction. And they said that they did not feel safe and that they didn't want to come. I personally went to Ilok, and upon my persistent instance, the three-member commission came in Sarengrad, and you can see here that they saw some civilians with hunting rifles, that they saw a lot of destruction there. They took photos. I don't know whether that remains anywhere. I asked them to go to Bapska with me. They said that they didn't feel safe. They returned to Ilok with the promise that they would do their utmost to stop further aggression. Unfortunately, I don't think that they succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I please tender 65 ter 2241 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I think it should be 2214, and that's already been admitted, as I understand it, as P321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Ms. Dennehy, you said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Mr. President. I do get my numbers mixed up. Can I please ask that 65 ter 5016.2 be shown. This is a video, and the time stamp, for the record, is 30:10 to 32:10. And there won't be any audio for the purposes of this video. It is only the scenes on which I will rely. I'm just being told that the exhibit number is 2024. It's Exhibit 2024.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: As I said, there is no audio for this clip required. It is only the images on which I will rely.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, did you recognise the scenes of the video that were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I was not in the convoy but did I recognise some persons, two people from Sarengrad. Nikola Lukic and Emil Rimar. I know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- Lukic, the man who was situated next to the baby in the video --

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: -- that is at paragraph -- at time stamp 31.42 for the record. Can you repeat in this name again, please.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nikola Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. And the convoy that you saw at time stamp 31.17 of vehicles, what was that convoy of?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: That was a convoy which was based on the ultimatum. People were saving their own lives. The citizens of Ilok, Sarengrad and Bapska and all those places that had previously fled to Ilok were given the right to carry only the bare necessities. They were not allowed to take any valuables with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric, now moving onto paragraph 18 of your statement, you say that: "My parents stayed in Sarengrad. They experienced a lot of bad things." When did your parents leave Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Most of those who remained in Sarengrad, and we're talking about elderly people who were not afraid as the rest of them, they basically lived in delusion because they knew some people from the JNA. They expected help from them, but just the opposite happened. My parents remained there. They didn't know whether I was alive or dead. They stayed on for another five months in Sarengrad. They experienced a lot of problems. And then when the citizens of Sarengrad and the surrounding places in March 1991 had to sign statements that they were leaving all of their property to the authorities in Eastern Slavonia and all the valuables, money and the rest they had to surrender, they signed that statement in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you've just told us that it was March 1991. That is, before the attack on Sarengrad. Would you like to look at that date again and see whether you'd like to change it?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It was in 1992. Not before the attack, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: So you mean March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, when did you return to Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of May, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did you observe in the schools in Sarengrad at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: On that day, when I returned, I was the deputy mayor of Ilok. I took over 200-plus elderly and frail Serbs in the Franciscan monastery. I found 232 children of whom 225 were Serb children, and most of those children were settled there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. And what happened to the two houses that you had in Sarengrad while you were away from the village?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: The house where I and my wife resided with my children was in the same street as my parents' house. When my parents were chased from that house, it was razed to the ground, and when I returned in 1997, I found an elderly family from Vocin living in that second house. The courtyard was very neglected and overgrown. The entire surroundings of the house were rather overgrown and neglected.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. You said that you found an elderly family from Vocin living in your second house. Where is Vocin?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Vocin is in Western Slavonia in the county of Virovitica and Zupanija.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The county of Virovitica and Podravina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, the family from Vocin, do you know what ethnicity that family was?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now ask that 65 ter 6133 be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you will see a final document on the screen in front of you. Looking at page 2 of this document, and this is a report from Tomislav Papic to the regional council of the SAO SBWS regarding the handing out of vacant houses in Ilok to refugees. Mr. Coric, at page 2 it says: "Ilok Croats left Ilok in large numbers on the 17th of October." And further down it says: "Refugees from Western Slavonia and other war-affected areas arrived successively and move into the unoccupied houses and flats."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the interpreters do not have the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we have the right document on the screen, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, this is the correct document, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: So at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And where -- where do we read --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: On page 2 of this document, you see question 7 says: "Return of local Croats to Sarengrad, how is this [sic] to be handled?" Mr. Coric, do you see this question in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Given your parents' experience, was it realistic that Croats returned to Ilok in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It was not realistic. This document precedes the day when the largest group were forcibly moved out of Sarengrad and the surrounding places. In this document, you can see that a bus arrives daily bringing Serbs from Western Slavonia, so try and imagine what those people could bring with them. They could only bring their bare necessities. As for the rest, they plundered the houses of those who had left them. The trend of the arrival of people from Western Slavonia was something that -- that dictated a number of those who had to leave their houses. On several occasions, people came to my late parents' house to see the condition that the house was in, and then eventually somebody pointed a finger and said, I want to move in. My father had to yield several hundred marks. He also had a silver stopwatch that me and my sister had bought him as a present. However, he had to give that to somebody to be allowed to leave the place where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. And now looking at the first page of this document, it's dated 14 March 1992. Does that date coincide with the time that your parents were forced to leave Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, it coincides, and a few days later they left Sarengrad, that is, Ilok, and through Sid they were taken to Bosnia, and by way of Slavonski Samac they entered Slavonski Brod. I was a member of the Croatian Army at the time and I personally came to meet them when they arrived Zagreb on a bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The Prosecution would ask that this 65 ter 6133 now be admitted into evidence. And that concludes my questions for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And that was, indeed -- I heard you say that this was your final document, so that was why we are a little bit over time. But basically that's good timing. Mr. Witness, Mr. Coric, this is the time for our first break. 30 minutes. We come back at 11.00. And, at that moment, Mr. Gosnell will start his cross-examination. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll be back at 11.05. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we remove the statement from the -- in front of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell, and I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings. I will ask you a few questions today. If any of my questions come through to you as unclear, then please feel free to ask for clarification or a restatement of my question, and I'll -- I'll do my best. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You told us earlier today that you were a founding member of the a political party. Can you tell us again the name of that political party?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I was a member of two political parties, but you are properly more interested in the one from 1989. I was a founder member of the Croatian Democratic Union in the former municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Have you been a member of any other party?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, later. The HSP. Not before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Party of Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when did you join that party?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I joined it in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you still a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: There were two factions in that party. Four and a half years ago, I -- I separated my faction, and my party is today called the HSP, Dr. Ante Starcevic, and I'm the general secretary. We also have a member of European Parliament from our party. That's Ms. Ruza Tomasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did Ms. Tomasic recently declare that Croatia is for Croats only. All the others are guests?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I think you're referring to an excerpt from a speech of hers. I was present at that rally at Slatina. The media took that out of context. She never stated it that way. She explained on a few occasions for the media, she meant to say that whoever lives in Croatia should respect it or leave. But that didn't refer to any particular minority or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It referred to all the minorities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No. Not any minority and not all minorities. She was speaking about Croatia. Croatia is inhabited by Croats, and they can be then divided into groups by religious affiliation and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the latter part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters did not get the last part of your answer. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which part they are referring to, but I'll try. In our programme, we do not divide the inhabitants of Croatia into minorities. We only see honest and dishonest people, but certainly, no, we don't distinguish by ethnicity. This interpretation of her statement was taken out of context. We don't stand behind any such ideas as a party, nor do we think that any minority should leave Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, can you explain what context gives a different meaning to the words "Croatia is for Croats only"?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasic lived in a developed democracy for 25 years. She lived in Canada. She graduated from a police academy and she respects the law and abides by it. She knows how democracy works, whereas the rest of us only had a chance to experience it in the last 20 years. So she actually said that in Canada, the people living there are Canadians. In Croatia, you will find Croatians and so on, and people should act that accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you a founding member of the -- of this party, the HSP?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I am the first founder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you tell us - and you may have already implicitly already answered this question but I would like to know - can you tell us specifically when the party first came into existence, if you can, the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: If we're speaking about the HSP, Dr. Ante Starcevic, the party was officially registered in October 2009. The founding assembly was held at Bapska, near my house, and I did so on purpose. There were a few hundred delegates. All other parliamentary parties in Croatia were founded in Zagreb but I wanted to show that our party cares about everybody in Croatia, not only about the capital. Officially our party was founded on the 6th of October --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Witness, the interpreters missed the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And before founding and participating in the founding of this party, were you a member of the HSP?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when was that party founded; and when did you become a member of the HSP?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: That party was founded over 160 years ago. It was prohibited occasionally. I believe that it was in 2001 that I was no longer satisfied with the policy of the HDZ after the death of President Tudjman and then I left that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What was it about the platform of the HDZ that did not satisfy you? In other words, what motivated you to participate in the founding of a new party?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: The basic motivation was when the cat's away, the mice will play. When the late president died, there -- there began an internal struggle for power and the members started to care more about form than about the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is your current party and before that the HSP, are they closely affiliated, in terms of outlook and ideology with another party called Hrvatska Cista Stranka Prava, the Hrvatska Pure Party of Rights?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: The oldest political world view in Croatia is the so-called Pravastvo and one of the parties advocating that is the HCSP. We ran together with the HCSP in the last electoral campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right that your current party, as well as the HSP and the HCSP, these parties together would be considered less moderate than the HDZ party; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how would you characterise this wing of the political spectrum?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Our political spectrum is conservative, Christian democrats. I personally as general secretary never allowed anybody to treat us as the so-called political right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D486, please, which is tab -- Defence tab 4. It's a document recently added to our list, and I sincerely hope that it's been released in e-court. Apparently it hasn't. I'll have to come back to this document, thank you, Mr. Registrar [sic]. Could I kindly ask that hard copies of the witness's statement be distributed to the legal officer and to the Judges if there's no opposition from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that a document you just asked to remove from the witness's desk in the beginning of your cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And is it the one with the paragraph numbers or without?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, with paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: With. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would ask that the witness then be provided with a copy if everyone else has a copy of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That's precisely the purpose of exercise we're about to undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you gave the statement that you looked at earlier today to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor 18 years ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I don't mean any criticism of you in saying this, but is it possible that as you sit here today, you have forgotten some of the things that you wrote down with that investigator 18 years ago?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I don't think I've forgot anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did you leave Sarengrad following the JNA attack?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I left Sarengrad on the 14th of October in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when did the women and children leave?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: My wife gave birth to a daughter on the -- on Saint Ann's day on the 26th of July, 1995, at Vinkovci hospital which was practically being shelled and they left Eastern Slavonia. My late brother came to fetch them in August --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: My wife and three children, among them a newborn, only five days old.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that we -- the LiveNote appears to have been interrupted. I will proceed because I have the screen in front of me, but it would be helpful if that could be fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We call the technician, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, I'm not sure that you answered my question. My question was: When did the women and children -- I'm not talking just about your wife when she went to give birth. I'm talking about the balance of the population of women and children in Sarengrad, when did they leave?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If I understood well, the organised -- there was no organised transportation of women and children from Sarengrad. They were taken from the monastery and other cellars during the night on the 4th of October, before the main attack. So we transported women, children, and the elderly to Ilok. There must have been 500 to 700 persons in all. There was shooting by the main road, and that's why we went through the woods from the monastery. We took them to the hill above Sarengrad, and there were two buses from Ilok public transportation. I remember Vinko Raguz with a private truck, too. And that's how we took them to Ilok. Among them, there were nuns, 21 Carmelites, and the parish priest was also there. Overnight, they were put up at the monastery at Ilok. And a smaller number of civilians went to their homes occasionally because they still had livestock there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. So was it the night of the 4th or the night of the 5th that this evacuation of women and children took place?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was on the night of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, that's paragraph 11 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Some days later, was someone killed in a town called Sotin?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who, and when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It's hard for me to give you a date because I would have to take a look at the document. It's my deputy Kresimir Djakovic. He was charged with supplying the population who was -- that was at Sarengrad with bread from Ilok. Somebody told him that the JNA and the paramilitaries had left Sotin and with a woman from Sotin who was dis -- displaced at Sarengrad and he took her to Sotin in his car. But that was a mistake because between Opatovac and Sotin the so-called JNA shot at them, killing him and wounding her. That's all I know about that because at the time we didn't have reliable information. He simply went missing. Only when we came to the free territory we found -- we got all the information about the way he lost his life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at some point, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, that's paragraph 12 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at some point, Mr. Coric, you managed to pass into Serbia. Could you please tell us where you went, once you had crossed the border and passed into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: In rough lines, I described that path of mine. I don't want to mention some people because they still live in Serbia today. After the referendum and after the signing of the agreement at Sid, it was clear that Ilok would be surrendered and that the civilian population would be deported in a convoy --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Coric, perhaps we could cut this short because we do have your statement. All the details are in there. I wouldn't wish to have you repeat all of that. The specific detail that I am interested in is where did you go once you crossed the border when you were in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It -- what I said matters to me for the reason that if I had been on the convoy, I would be taken out and probably killed, not even taken to a camp. My deputies and the others were taken out of the convoy and taken to a camp and being mistreated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness. Mr. Witness, could you please answer the specific question Mr. Gosnell put to you or say that you don't -- you don't remember if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember. I'm merely explaining my reasons. I arrived at Sid. There is a restaurant by the name of Cubura, and the son of Petar Vidakovic took me to Belgrade. He was in civilian clothes. And I got on a train in Belgrade, rode to Subotica and met some friends there. They took me to the Hungarian border in a car, and by way of Hungary, I went -- travelled on to Munich, then to Vienna, and returned to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when did you arrive back in Zagreb after this itinerary?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While you were in Sarengrad -- well, let me just ask again. When did you say that you left -- strike that. While you were in Sarengrad, was there a Croatian soldier who swam the Danube River to reach Sarengrad? And can you please describe that event.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: The members of the civilian protection that were standing guard along the Danube, sometime around the 10th or -- or rather, four, five days before the fall of Ilok and Sarengrad, saw somebody that had swam across the Danube. They found a frozen JNA soldier who was a Croatian from Australia. He confirmed the story for us. They were told to shoot at us. He was the victim of the propaganda war, according to which there were thousands upon thousands of Ustasha who were slaughtering children, ill-treating Serbian population, and all of them were across the Danube. As a Croatian, he decided to leave the army and then he saw some dozen of us poorly dressed without any weapons. He cried. He was in no position to hold any duties. On that day we gave him civilian clothes. We transferred him to the monastery in Ilok. There he was with our nuns. Since there was a police station in Ilok, they made him fake ID papers and he used those papers to join the convoy as a civilian. Later on I heard that, in 1993, that soldier was killed as a Croatian soldier. During all the negotiations that our commission participated in, there were two ultimatums that we were given. One of them was to surrender the tank, and from Ilaca it ended up in a forest near Ilok. And all the time they kept on asking us where that soldier was, the one who had swam the river. And obviously we did not want to surrender him to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to have to mention this, but we've lost the transcript server again and access to e-court. I'm not sure whether that can be fixed. I can proceed but ...
