utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you do whatever it takes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I have it back now. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, how many Serbs were living in the town of -- or the village of Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: According to the last census, which took place in 1991, Sarengrad had 1150 inhabitants, and there were less than 10 per cent Serbs. Not more than 80 to 90 all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is paragraph 4 of the statement for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were there any members of the civilian defence force that was set up in Sarengrad? Excuse me, let me clarify my question. Were there any Serb members of the civilian defence force?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the civilian protection was not a military formation. We were not trained. We didn't have any weapons. Everybody who joined, joined voluntarily. Among them were Milivoj Radojcin, Bratus, and Jovan Kovacevic, who personally reported to me and said that they wanted to participate in all the activities pertaining to the protection of the village and we gladly took them on. The other Serbs did not want to join. On our part, we did not put any pressure on them to bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you sure you didn't have any weapons that were used for the civilian defence force?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: We did have weapons, but not enough, not enough for a hundred people to be armed properly. We had hunting rifles, which is confirmed by the statement of the UN commission that was in Sarengrad and that was able to establish the nature of the weapons. Some of the -- the rifles had been purchased. Those were shotguns whose range was about 50 metres. We had some automatic weapons, pistol and others that were purchased on the black market from the smugglers who toured the area daily. I think I saw in some documents that one had to fork out 500 to 1200 German marks to buy a rifle. People did not have enough money. Some sold their cows in order to buy rifles which they considered their own personal weapons. Those weapons had to be under control on the premises of the local commune. This means that those weapons were never taken to any lines or they were all under my control. Nobody among the Serbs in Sarengrad were not as much as insulted as long as being physically ill treated [as interpreted]. We were very rigorous there, and I personally take proud of that part of -- of our life there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you did have weapons that were used for the civilian defence force.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Than included automatic rifles; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Very few, yes. A fewer number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you provided with any money from the HDZ to purchase weapons?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No. I was the HDZ, together with some other people, and we did not have any money for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You didn't participate in a meeting in July or August 1990 at which the HDZ, in particular Tomislav Mercep, discussed arming groups of Croats in villages?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I was at that meeting. If you're referring to the meeting at Bogdanovci. There were several hundred citizens there. There were all civilians. Nobody wore a uniform. Nobody had a rifle or a pistol. That Tomislav Mercep gave a motivating speech. He gave people -- that we would survive, that we would defend ourselves, that we would receive assistance from the west. We always believed that the Americans would be on our side. We lived in an illusion and that's how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At the meeting at Bogdanovci -- well, first of all, precisely when was that meeting, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I know that before that we managed to stop tanks in Bogdanovci with our bodies. The tanks wanted to pass through Bogdanovci in the direction of Vukovar. We gathered and with other our own bodies we prevented their passage, and that was our motive to try and gather our forces and organise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that in 1990 or 1991, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was in 1991, but I'm really not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How long before the incident in Borovo Selo when Croatian policemen were killed did that occur, or was it after?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I took the oath, so I don't want to say something wrong. I was at the meeting. There is a video-clip which can be easily obtained. You can see who those people were, and you can see that none -- none of them were soldiers. It was -- it was not a military formation of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there any discussion of setting up HDZ armed formations in towns at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: When you are in power in a town like we were in Bogdanovci and Ilok, you had obligations. When -- one of those obligations is to protect the population and their property, first and foremost, as I've already tried to tell you, the equipment and the weapons were stored at the Secretariat for National Defence in Vukovar and that was under the control of the Serbian side and the SDS. When we managed to reach those premises we found empty depots where once thousands upon thousands of rifles had been. So that that was our obligation. That was what we wanted to do. We wanted to contribute towards the defence and protection of the population and its property. The only thing that existed at the time was the HDZ. And in keeping with that, obviously the HDZ was the generating force behind all of the events. At that time we could not work on the development of the economy. We had to deal with the aggression that had already started and that had already reached our door-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see once again that the witness has strayed into territory that was covered by Your Honours' ruling. And nothing in the question that I posed leaned in that direction. I was inclined before I started the cross-examination not to go back to this subject, but now I would seek your guidance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Why don't you stop the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm listening -- I'm listening on translation, and it would have been impossible to cut him off before he said what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we would like you to give, as far as possible, short answers and precise answers to the questions, to precise questions. Could you try to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I ask for your guidance. I would wish to put a simple proposition to the witness on this subject, but I wouldn't wish to open the floor to an endless cross-examination on the topics. And since the witness has blurted it out twice, I would ask for your latitude to put a proposition but not have that proposition open the door to material that we say is just improper for having heard from this witness. But I'm in Your Honours' hands as to whether that is permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The Prosecution would object to this. It is, first of all, not clear what my learned friend would like to lead cross-examination on from his recent statement. We were also precluded from and we did follow the Trial Chamber's guide-lines in respect of what was permissible in terms of our examination-in-chief, and we don't think that it's appropriate or proper at this time that the Defence would then be allowed to circumvent that ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that what you're trying to do, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours can give me an assurance that the two statements that have been made about the SDS allegedly being -- what he has now said on cross is that the SDS was in charge of the Committee for National Defence and what he said during his chief was that the SDS was in charge of the TO depots. Two different things. If Your Honours can reassure me that those are not in evidence, then I won't seek to embark on any questions on this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will not rely on the witness's evidence on these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, what was Tomislav Mercep's position leading up to the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to be succinct. In 1989 I met the first Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman, in Stuttgart, in a Catholic mission. I joined the HDZ very soon thereafter. And then I attended a meeting with Branimir Glavas and Vladimir Seks at the Bendek restaurant in Osijek --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, Mr. Coric. I'm guided by the Chamber's instructions to me to do my best to ensure that you answer the question. So could I kindly ask you to just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And to speak slowly, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I'm trying to say a lot as quickly as I can. I was appointed the co-ordinator of the HDZ for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's not helpful, Mr. Coric --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to tell you how Tomislav Mercep got involved. Without those two sentences I can't get to the bottom of the whole matter. Tomislav Mercep did not fall out of the sky. I have to tell you how we functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: When I -- when I said that that was not helpful Mr. Coric, I meant, in the first place, you're speaking as fast as you can. That's not helpful. Now, the other -- the other issue is whether you should expand or not. Try to be as short as possible but, of course, you need to answer the question eventually with a little bit of context. But please speak slowly. Perhaps you could repeat the question, Mr. Gosnell, so that we are back on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Coric, the question was: What was Mr. Mercep's position prior to the outbreak of hostilities in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: As the HDZ co-ordinator for Vukovar, I was looking for people whom I could include. I tried to get hold of highly educated people. I heard of Tomislav Mercep as an engineer who worked at the Borovo. My best man worked there. I asked for a meeting. I came to [Mercep's house, I explained to him who we were, what our programme and plan were. That was in 1989. He then introduced me to his best man, the late Blago Zadro. I asked them to come to Sarengrad on the 30th of December, 1989, where the inception meeting of the HDZ for that part of Slavonia would take place. That was on the 30th of December, 1989. He -- I asked him to come to Sarengrad to hear what we had to say. They did come. And during the break and during the secret ballot at which I was elected as the first president of the HDZ, they officially became members themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry -- sorry, maybe we can just focus this. Between January 1st, 1990, and August 1991, can you just tell us the titles, if you know, of the positions held by Mr. Mercep?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: When he became a member, he was the first branch president in Bogdanovci. That was on the 10 February 1990. And very soon he imposed himself as a -- as a leader and he became president for the municipality of Vukovar, the president of the HDZ. Before he left Vukovar in August 1991, he had been appointed the secretary of the Secretariat for the National Defence of Vukovar. When he became secretary, we found empty depots and everything else that I've already mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You're sure it was August 1991? Or was it, in fact, earlier than August 1991 that Mr. Mercep became the secretary of the committee for national defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It was much earlier. He had been the secretary for a few months before he left Vukovar in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In what month did he become secretary of the committee for national defence?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Hard to say. Perhaps in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Possibly even before the incident in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there any ZNG armed unit or presence in Sarengrad at any time up until the time of your departure on the 14th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: There was a platoon of the ZNG, as you called them. They were members of the 1st Guards Brigade, the so-called Tigers. They spent ten or perhaps 15 days in Sarengrad in the month of June. Then they went to Ilok. And they were billeted in Principovac. In all the subsequent events, neither that unit nor any other unit participated in anything in Sarengrad. They did not take part in anything surrounding the aggression or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you say that there was no ZNG armed presence in Sarengrad on the 4th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, this is paragraph 8 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you gave your interview in 1995, were you asked whether there was any ZNG presence in Sarengrad at any time, whether it be June, July, August, September, or October 1991?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I don't need to say anything that's not true. I believe that I said the same thing then that I'm saying today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recall that you mentioned that there was a ZNG armed presence at some point in time during that period?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I have repeated that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet that doesn't appear in your statement. That's my proposition to you.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Maybe they did not deem that to be necessary or of essence. It is a well-known fact that two members of the 1st Guards Brigade of the so-called ZNG, or at least that's what you call them, were killed in Sarengrad, but they were killed by a shell while they were in their car. They were driving from Bapska. They were in -- to Ilok. They were in the car of the late Ilok veterinarian. The shell hit them in the centre of Sarengrad. The two of them were killed. Another one was seriously wounded. He lost his arm and a leg. We handed him over on the bridge to the so-called JNA. Later on, I heard that he was transported to Novi Sad and that he has survived. That was our only contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What date did that occur, that they were injured? Sorry, that one was injured and one was killed.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Actually, two were killed. Lovric and Gudelj. Two were killed; one was wounded on the 4th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were they armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I believe that they had side-arms or something of the kind in the car. But that was the last of our worries at the time. At the scene that I saw there was really ugly, because they suffered a direct hit. The shell hit the car directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why were they there on their own? Or were they on their own?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: There were three of them in the car. I didn't know that there would -- they would be there. Many others tried to zoom through the village during the shelling from one side to the other. Some got lucky. The three of them didn't. As far as I know, they were not on any special mission in Sarengrad or anywhere near. One of the big misconceptions about the ZNG was that they were trained militarily. It's simply not true. The two that were killed were just two young lads who did not have anything whatsoever to do, either with war or the military or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, then, how did you know them to be members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I know their names, and I was the one who erected a monument at the place where they were killed. They were in uniforms. Therefore, unfortunately, we had to load them onto a small tractor. We took them to the far end of the village. We loaded them into an ambulance. They were transferred to Ilok. I don't know what happened next. And we went back to our own business, which was saving the houses that were on fire and people who had been wounded. It was only much later that I learnt the names of the people who had been killed. I learned their names only when I returned to Sarengrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you speak to them prior to the event of them being injured?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No. They were killed about an hour after the most fierce shelling had started. We did not have Motorolas or any means of communication. We did not have telephone lines. We did not have electricity. Everything was down. So there was no way for us to communicate with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Weren't they there assisting in the defence of Sarengrad at that time, militarily?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Isn't the reason that you evacuated the women and children on the 4th of October was precisely so that you could defend that town militarily with minimum civilian casualties? Isn't that precisely why they were evacuated and you didn't leave at the same time?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It was my duty as commander of the civil protection to help the civilians, which I did. Whoever wanted to leave, I made it possible for them. But I left and if there had been an infantry attack on Sarengrad, we would have put up resistance with the few weapons that we had. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "I stayed," not "I left."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My parents stayed in Sarengrad all the time. Nobody -- or, rather, we wouldn't have allowed any criminals to come in without my trying to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you were bracing for an infantry attack against Sarengrad, and you organised, in accordance with your responsibilities in the civilian protection, you organised the defence of the town accordingly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: In keeping with our delusions and given the poor equipment that we had, once we set up -- when we're setting up the civil protection we didn't know that the JNA had sided with the aggressor and the paramilitaries. Instead, we expected an infantry attack, that there would be infiltrated groups attempting to commit crimes and burn down houses. And so we were willing to protect ourselves to the extent we could with the few weapons that we had. I believe these are rights guaranteed by the Geneva Conventions, among others. I am afraid that our resistance would have been weak and short, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many weapons did you have? How many of you were armed in preparing this defence?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I said that during those months until the fall, we had a total of 100 men -- people taking part in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just clarify and narrow my question. After the 4th of October - let's specifically restrict ourselves to that - how many of you were armed in defence of Sarengrad?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Not more than 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And no one from the ZNG assisted you?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No one. No one wanted to come to Sarengrad. Neither the police, nor the ZNG, nor the international community, or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you request the assistance of the ZNG or the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I couldn't. There was no way. Those first few days, I told you, whoever was wounded had to die or was surrendered to the enemy. Everything else was boiled down to a struggle for survival. Because we soon realised that there would be no infantry attack, that we would be shelled day and night from heavy weapons, and morale soon sank. We were soon left without electricity. We were the ones supplying the population with bread. We were releasing the livestock for it not to starve to death --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm just going to move to the next question if that's all right with everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, what is your current position in the HSP, Dr. Ante Starcevic Party. What position do you hold?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: General secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that an elected office?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody is elected in our party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I mean to say are you elected by the population?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: One of the political duties that I hold is the -- is president of the local committee of Sarengrad. I got --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the percentage of votes he got.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could you repeat how many -- what percentage of votes you received.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: 69 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in the -- amongst those who you represent, do you represent individuals of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D486, please, which now should be uploaded and ready for release on e-court. And if we could please zoom in on the section entitled: "Thieves and Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that Ms. Tomasic, the one who we identified -- or that you identified earlier as the leader of your party, the party of which you are a member?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Here's what she is reported to have said. Well, perhaps I could ask you to read it because my translation, the one that I provided may not be perfect. Could you please read the sentences, two sentences, the first one beginning: "It's time to loudly tell the truth ..."

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: It's very small. Could it be enlarged?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's try, if we can, to switch only to the B/C/S version and zoom in on the part below: "Lopovi i Cetnici."

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can start with: "It's time to loudly tell the truth ..."

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: "'It is time to tell the truth aloud that a Croat today, in spite of everything, may say in Croatia that a thief is a thief and a Chetnik is a Chetnik,' Tomasic said." Need I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: "Tomasic said and promised that this co-operation with the HDZ party would be to everybody's benefit, mostly to the benefit of the citizens. Tomasic announced a return of the system that was abolished long ago in order to hide the truth and pointed out that Croatia is for Croats and everybody else are guests."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How was that comment received amongst the audience?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: First of all, I must express my reservations towards this shortened statement of hers because it does not reflect the truth of what she said. It was recorded on video, by the way. Ms. Tomasic certainly did not refer to any minority. In Vukovar we have -- also have ethnic Serbs who run on our list. My party, for example, won in Miklusevci, Tompojevci, and Petrusevci [phoen], with members of Ruthenian and Ukrainian -- who are members of those minorities. This is a falsified statement, but having said all that, I must say that I agree with what she said. A thief is a thief; and a Chetnik is a Chetnik. Both Ms. Tomasic and I are known for speaking out the truth without mincing our words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And leaving aside whatever additional words she may have uttered during this meeting, did she utter the words that are reported in this article?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is the journalist's free interpretation. I don't know which media this was published in. That's the journalist's conclusion. We explained these statements on a number of occasions. They were taken out of the context of her entire speech and now this sounds very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you denying that she said, "A thief is a thief; a Chetnik is a Chetnik"? And are you denying that she said -- well, let's start there. Do you deny that? Did she say that?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do apologise for interrupting. However, the witness has already responded to that particular question. He has said, actually, at line 18 of page 62, that he agreed with that. And so this is repetition of the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe my learned friend may have given an erroneous line reference or page reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The LiveNote in front of me at page 61, line 18, says: "This is a falsified statement, but having said that, I must say that I agree with what she said. A thief is a thief; and a Chetnik is a Chetnik." That was the witness's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly ambiguous, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is there ambiguous about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether in indicating that it's a falsified statement, this is in line with his claim that the journalist has taken it out of context or whether the witness is saying that she didn't say those things. In fact, I understood earlier that he indicated earlier that she did say these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may ask the question to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did she say those words: "A thief is a thief; and a Chetnik is a Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did she say Croatia ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Something appears to be missing from the LiveNote, Mr. President. It was the translation of the other portion. May I put that to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have it here on the screen. "Croatia for the Croats," and then the only -- but there we have to go over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just put it like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did she say that Croatia is for Croats and all the others are guests?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Not in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I could conclude in two questions, depending on the answers, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did -- have you spoken to anyone about your impending testimony here before the ICTY, before you travelled here?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You told no one in your party that you were coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No. They know I was going to The Hague, but I never speak about my statement, with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did any of them suggest that you should testify in a particular way, even in a joking manner?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Have you spoken to any public officials about your upcoming testimony?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you feel any motivation to testify in a particular way, because if you were to say anything favourable to Mr. Hadzic, you would be blamed for that in your party?

utterances.speaker: PERO CORIC
utterances.text: Not like that. I only feel the need to tell the truth so that it may become known. That is my motivation: To tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This document is tendered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D74, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, of course, we'll seek a proper translation of the document for uploading to e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then I would perhaps admit it -- MFI it, pending translation, right, or pending correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did get to my feet or attempted to get to my feet. But I presumed that given the time, you wouldn't have decided or that the Trial Chamber wouldn't have decided on whether the -- the admissibility of this document. The Prosecution objects to the admission of this document on the basis that the witness has not provided proper -- a proper foundation for it, and has actually said that he disagrees with the foundation and the opinion stated in this document and he believes that it's untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You should be less hesitant with getting on your feet, Ms. Dennehy. Because I saw indeed a slight movement and then you sat down again.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Given the proximity to the break, I thought that Your Honours were going to break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness was present during the meeting reported in the article. The witness confirmed at least two passages that are cited in the article, even though he may disagree with the overall presentation, and that's enough for admission and foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Is there anything in re-direct, Ms. Dennehy? If there is, I think we better take the break, but -- unless you say I have only one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: No, I have nothing in re-direct at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have nothing in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, this is the end of your testimony. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You're now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey home. The court usher will escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There's nothing else for today?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a procedural issue that I would like to address in relation to the exhibits that were tendered earlier. This is just for the record. That is, that Exhibit P2277 should be assigned -- or excuse me. Exhibit 65 ter 414.3 should be assigned to Exhibit P2277. And exhibit 65 ter 414.4 is assigned P2978. And those just the break -- the 2278. I apologise. Those are the -- the exhibits tendered earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Noted. Thank you. If nothing else, court adjourned for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of June, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.22 p.m.,
